paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Pearls have always held special status among the rich and powerful. Women in ancient Rome, for example, reportedly wore pearls to bed so that, on waking, they would be reminded of their wealth. Pearls had greater commercial value than diamonds until jewellers learnt to cut gemstones. In Eastern countries such as Persia, ground pearl powder was used as medicine for ailments ranging from heart disease to epilepsy.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Pearls can generally be divided into three categories: natural, cultured and imitation. When an irritant, such as a grain of sand, enters a certain type of oyster, mussel or clam, the mollusc secretes a defensive fluid to coat it. Layers gradually accumulate around the irritant until a lustrous natural pearl forms.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A cultured pearl undergoes the same process, with one difference: the irritant is a bead called ‘mother-of-pearl’, surgically implanted in the oyster. This produces a much larger core in cultured pearls than in natural ones. As long as enough layers of nacre—the secreted fluid coating the irritant—form a beautiful, gem-quality pearl, the nucleus’s size does not affect its beauty or durability.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Pearls come from both saltwater and freshwater sources. Saltwater pearls are typically of high quality, although some freshwater pearls are also highly regarded. Freshwater pearls often have irregular, puffed-rice shapes. Nevertheless, individual qualities determine a pearl’s value more than its source. Saltwater pearl oysters are usually cultivated in protected lagoons or volcanic atolls, while most freshwater cultured pearls sold today come from China. Producers have several options: they may use freshwater or saltwater shellfish, place a graft in the mantle or gonad, add a spherical bead or use no bead.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Whichever method is used, producing pearls usually takes several years. Mussels must mature, which can take almost three years, before an irritant is implanted. The pearl then requires approximately another three years to reach full size. Sometimes the irritant is rejected; the pearl may become badly deformed or the oyster may die from complications such as disease. At the end of a five- to ten-year cycle, only half the oysters may have survived. Of the pearls eventually produced, only about 5% are of sufficiently high quality for jewellers.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Imitation pearls are another matter. The island of Mallorca in Spain is renowned for its imitation-pearl industry. In most cases, a bead is dipped in a solution made from fish scales, but the resulting coating is thin and often wears away. One way to distinguish an imitation is to rub it gently against the teeth: fake pearls feel smooth, whereas the layers of nacre on real pearls feel gritty.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Several factors are considered when evaluating a pearl: size, shape, colour, surface quality and lustre. In descending order of value, the three types are natural, cultured and imitation, the last of which is essentially worthless. To determine whether a pearl is natural or cultured, jewellers can send it to a gem laboratory for an X-ray. High-quality natural pearls are extremely rare. Japan’s Akoya pearls are among the most lustrous available, while the southern seas around Australia produce larger pearls.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Historically, the world’s highest-quality pearls came from the Persian Gulf, particularly the waters around Bahrain. Divers harvested them by hand without advanced equipment. The discovery of large oil reserves in the early 1930s, however, brought the Persian Gulf’s natural-pearl industry to an abrupt end when contaminated water destroyed the once-pristine beds. Today, India probably holds the largest stock of natural pearls. Ironically, much of that stock originally came from Bahrain.
